title: The Core of OOP: Composition Over Inheritance

scenes.line1: Why do top engineers avoid deep
scenes.say: Why do the best engineers almost never build deep inheritance trees?

scenes.label: Inheritance
scenes.sub: Classes extend each other in long chains.
scenes.say: Traditional object-oriented code often stacks classes on top of each other, creating long inheritance chains.
But composition flips this. Instead of rigid hierarchies, you build classes by combining smaller objects. That means less coupling and more flexibility.
This idea is at the heart of the S O L I D principles. Each class has one job, you extend without rewriting, and you depend on interfaces, not details.
See here? The Service class gets a Logger. It doesn't inherit from it. You can swap in any logger you want, even a mock for tests.

scenes.question: Should you always use inheritance?
scenes.right: No. Prefer composition for flexibility and maintainability.
scenes.say: Here's a trap: thinking inheritance is always best for reusing code. In reality, composition keeps your code flexible and much easier to maintain.
